Ralph Merkle patentó el árbol de hashes: Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979, for hash-based signatures. Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta published in 1991 the hash chain for time-stamping documents, and since 1995 they have published the weekly root in the New York Times. Adam Back proposed proof of work in 1997, Hashcash, against junk mail. Satoshi Nakamoto put the three things together in 2008 in the Bitcoin paper, whose bibliography cites Haber, Stornetta and Back.

It reads: “the hash of the block with the nonce has to be less than two to the two hundred and fifty-six minus d”: starting with $d$ zeros. Each attempt succeeds with probability $2^{-d}$, so the attempts follow a geometric distribution with mean $2^d$.

Checking it costs a single hash: the work is expensive to do and cheap to verify. The difficulty is adjusted every so often so that the rate of blocks holds even when the total power changes.

It reads: “the hash of block i is the hash of the previous hash concatenated with its data”. Changing a block's data changes its hash, and with it the next one's, and the next one's: to alter block 3 out of 1000 you have to redo the 998 that follow, and the last hash, which everybody has noted down, no longer matches.

The chain does not prevent alteration: it gives it away. It is evidence of tampering, not protection. What prevents rewriting is that redoing the blocks costs something, or that many people hold copies.
Si cualquiera puede rehacer los bloques,: If anybody can redo the blocks, the chain only gives away whoever cannot be bothered. Bitcoin's idea is that adding a block should cost something: the block has to carry a number, the nonce, such that its hash starts with $d$ zeros. Since the hash is unpredictable, the only way of finding it is to try nonces, and on average $2^d$ are needed. Rewriting the past requires redoing that work for every later block, faster than everybody else together adds new ones.
